title: The Bridge watches transcripts and captures a screen only when it can matter: an idle fleet costs no tmux call per agent per pass, and readiness is seen as soon as today
prompt:
Read, in crates/spawn-core/src/bridge.rs, `Bridge::tick` (the claim loop, then `act`), `act`, `follow_output` (each live transcript re-read from its offset on every tick, `READ_LIMIT`), `follow_screen` (a `capture_tail` of every live pane on every tick; a reading recorded only when two in a row agree and it changed, or after `screen_refresh` while busy), `BridgeConfig` (`lease_ttl`, `max_commands_per_tick`, `screen_refresh`) and the input path that captures the pane around typing (`type_once`, `PANE_NOT_READY`, `MAY_HAVE_TYPED`); `capture_tail` and `read_from` in crates/spawn-host/src/tmux.rs (a `tmux capture-pane` subprocess per call); `read_claude_screen` in crates/spawn-core/src/screen.rs; `claude_line` in crates/spawn-core/src/ingest.rs; `resident_loop` in crates/spawn-cli/src/commands/loops.rs and `loop_interval()` in crates/spawn-cli/src/config.rs; `held()` and the readiness rules (`idle_at_prompt`, `turn_stopped_idle`) in crates/spawn-cli/src/deliver.rs; the crates the gate can build offline: no inotify or notify crate is in ~/.cargo/registry, but libc 0.2.191 (already in Cargo.lock: `inotify_init1`, `inotify_add_watch`, `inotify_rm_watch`), rustix 1.1.6 (also in Cargo.lock; its `fs` feature has inotify) and nix 0.29/0.31 are; docs/design.md §5 (Agent Bridge), §6 (屏尾判定) and §14.

The problem. On every pass (500 ms) `spawn loop`'s Bridge runs one `tmux capture-pane` subprocess for every live session and re-reads every live transcript, serially, on the loop thread, and only then is the next command claimed. The cost grows with the fleet, not with what happens in it: twelve idle agents cost 274 pane captures in 30 s, and with each capture taking 50 ms (what a host running dozens of agents and their tmux server pays) a pass takes 1.3 s instead of 0.5, so a submitted command waits up to 1.7 s, 0.83 s on average, before the Bridge even claims it. Most of those captures read a screen nothing has touched: an idle engine's screen changes when its transcript does or when something is typed into it. The owner's goal (2026-11-06) is the Pareto frontier: no dimension improves by letting another regress, so no screen change that decides a delivery may be seen later than today.

Required behaviour (the contract the gate checks).
1. Transcripts are watched, not re-read. The Bridge watches each live session's transcript file (and the directory it will appear in) with inotify on Linux (the platform's equivalent elsewhere), and reads a transcript only when it changed since its last read; where no watch can be set (an error, an unsupported filesystem, a watch limit reached), that session falls back to today's read on every pass, said once in the loop's output. A line written while a read is in progress is read at the next change or pass, never lost: the offset rule of `follow_output` stays.
2. Screens are captured when they can matter. A live session's pane is captured on a pass only when (a) a command is in flight on it (claimed and not finished, or pending in the queue for it), or (b) its transcript has been quiet for SPAWN_SCREEN_QUIET_MS (default 500) since it last grew and the screen has not been read since, with readings repeated on the following passes until two in a row agree (the confirmation `follow_screen` needs today), or (c) at most once per `screen_refresh` (30 s) since its last capture, as a backstop for a screen that changes with no transcript (a dialog, a crash to a shell). A busy screen is still recorded again every `screen_refresh` while a turn keeps it busy. An idle session with a quiet transcript and nothing in flight costs no capture between backstops.
3. The tick is short. With the captures of (2) and the reads of (1), a pass over an idle fleet does no subprocess and no file read per agent; a command is claimed at the next pass, so it waits no longer than the pass interval and a tick.
4. Readiness as soon as today. Every screen change that decides a delivery (`held()`: the worker idle at its prompt, its turn stopped) is recorded no later than today: a waiting task is delivered within today's latency of its worker's turn's end. SPAWN_SCREEN_QUIET_MS is chosen for that, and the transcript's end of a turn (`turn.stopped`) is read as soon as the file changes.
5. Causality (§14): a screen state is recorded from a capture, a turn's end from the transcript's line; the absence of a capture or of a transcript change is never read as a state (a quiet transcript only says when to look at the screen again).

How the saving shows, in numbers. In the scenario (twelve idle residents, 50 ms captures): 272-276 captures in 30 s today, at most 24 allowed; claims today 134-1745 ms after creation (mean 815-838 ms), at most 750 ms allowed; deliveries of waiting tasks today 1742-1896 ms after the turn's end, at most 2500 ms allowed. On the live fleet a capture costs a fork and exec of tmux and a round trip to its server: about 2 per agent per second today, about one per agent per 30 s when idle. 017's scorecard has no dimension for the Bridge's load; lead time is its nearest, and must not grow: the scenario holds delivery readiness to today's latency.

State the rule in the module comment of bridge.rs, in docs/design.md §5 (what the Bridge reads, and when) and §6. Add unit tests: a session with a command in flight is captured every pass; one whose transcript grew is not captured until SPAWN_SCREEN_QUIET_MS of quiet, then until two readings agree, then not again until the backstop; the backstop and the busy refresh; a transcript change is read once per change and a line written mid-read is read at the next one; the polling fallback when a watch cannot be set (with a fake watcher), said once.

The gate judges this with rsi/scenarios/025.sh (read it: its header lists today's measures). A real `spawn loop` (no model judge, no supervisor, the default 500 ms interval) runs twelve residents, `r01` to `r12`, on a fake engine, all idle at their prompt; the tmux the loop runs is a wrapper that notes every call and makes each `capture-pane` cost 50 ms. It checks:
- (1) over 30 s of an idle fleet (every session waiting, nothing in flight, no transcript growing) the loop captures at most 24 panes;
- (2) twelve inputs, one to each resident, 2.3 s apart, are each claimed (`lease_until_ms` minus the two-minute lease) within 750 ms of their creation;
- (3) three residents are made busy (a turn of 8 s whose transcript grows every 2 s and whose screen shows the running turn) and a task assigned to each meanwhile; each task's delivery `deliver-<task>-0` is created within 2500 ms of the moment its engine ended the turn (the transcript's end of turn written, the prompt back), and goes through at that first attempt.
On the live main (49b92be; the deployed binary is built from it) it fails at (1): "(1) an idle fleet of 12 (every session waiting, nothing in flight, no transcript growing) had its panes captured 272 times in 30 s, more than 24: a tmux subprocess per agent per tick"; with BB_025_MEASURE=1 (only to show today's behaviour) it goes on and fails (2) (worst claim 1445-1745 ms) and passes (3) (1742-1896 ms), which is what the change must keep. It exits 0 when every check passes, 1 when an assertion fails, 2 on a harness failure.

Rules: never edit the protected paths, which the gate rejects: rsi/, scripts/ (scripts/rsi/, scripts/blackbox/, scripts/e2e.sh among them), deploy/, all of web/ except web/src/ and web/index.html, rust-toolchain files and .cargo/. The gate also rejects fewer runnable tests than the base (do not delete, rename, ignore or disable tests), any lint relaxation ([lints] tables, clippy.toml, a new crate-level #![allow]/#![expect], a removed #![warn]/#![deny]) and any build-time code (build.rs, .cargo/, a `build =` key in a Cargo.toml). The gate builds offline from the cargo caches already on the host: a new crate builds only if it is already in ~/.cargo/registry. Keep every existing check green (clippy -D warnings, the workspace tests, the e2e, the black-box scenarios, the web build) and add tests of your own for the new behaviour.
